Hut tour years later. on ! the advire of the !tenni of Ceremonies, lie withdrew . the edict, and left the ladies free to follow their 'own tastes. The origin al the strange custom metes to be lost in obscurity. In the eighth century of our era the wife of an Emperor of the Tang dynasty in mid to have worn shoes only three inches long, and one theory assigns Ike practice to thr fourth century an., "when Pan Pei danced before Ofe last of the Sovereigns of the Tel I dynasty, and every footetee made a lily grow." It in I also mid that it originated in the tenth :Meters, when a beautiful emieuhine of one of the Emperor. ',tied op her feet with silk into the shape of a crescent moon, and all the other beautim of the time imitated her." The older poets make no reference to the cramped foots hut sing of the beauty of the snow-white feet of the women of their tines, when the foot gear, when it wan , worn, was square-toed for men and round-toed for women. div.head: WITH THE HOP-PICKERS.
div.p: WITH THE HOP-PICKERS.
By F. Blacue

I had heard a great deal el the hop-picker, or, as I believe he preferA to be known, the " hopper,- and in my thirst for additional information, I thus had myself no the clock strikes twelve, waiting with a crowd of the objects of my curiosity Elr one of the big Hop-pickers' Excursions the Southern Railway Companies run during the first week in September, for the benefit of the poor of London in their autumn exodus to labour is that fantastic

fairyland of rural scenery, the hop-gardens of Southern England. It is a curious sight. Whole families, surrounded by their belongings, are lying about the stone pave- ment, some chatting merrily, some asleep, others taking careful stock of the luggage, that nothing may be left behind. Nat as large, by the way, this luggage ; usually only consisting of a blanket, kettle, saucepan, and a tin cup or two, packed roughly inn sack, something after the manner cu a sailor's kit. There are, however, exceptions to this. Some of the travellers, economically inclined, and having RR eye to probable rise in prices, come,- quent on the sudden invasion of a rural district, have laid in provisions also, among which. I judge from the prevailing aroma, the toothsome bloater I occupies a prominent place. A bustle, the ticket offices are open, and with the assistance of half-a-dozen policemen, and a score of railway officials to prevent crowding and to keep the MOB in order, booking goes on with inconceivable rapidity, while I learn some interesting facts about the traffic to the hop districts during the season There are something like 57,(JX) acres of hops this year under cultivation, but the acreage, under the competition of foreign hops, is steadily decreasing. Last year about 60,000 pickers wen down to the Kentish gardens alone. Of these about 40,000 were : conveyed by rail, 14,000 tramped, and another 1,000 I went by conveyance, presumedly like the donkey I cart, which with women and children enthroned in state, has just driven up. Of the pickers travel- ling by rail, the South Eastern Railway Company usually takes about 35,000, ruining sometimes thirteen or fourteen trains daily between midnight and 3 a.m. Sometimes on Saturday nights four or tire thousand pickers make the journey. This year competition among the pickers is fear- fully keen, probably on account of the strike which closes effectually the labour markets of the metropolis, and another thousand ie.ople have already gone out to the gardens. This traffic is,how- er, scarcely the profitable business to the railway , companies it appears at first sight. Of that 45,000 'travelling into Kent during the sea-on, it must not be imagined that all pay the full fare. Oh, dear no The child of three or touryears of age can pick, and the forty-live thousand for t most part go down in families, in which even the youngest member puts forth its skill to aid in the accumulation of a nerve fund against the coming of that grim enemy of the poor-- the winter. So many children "tinter age" go down, that in a train of 600 people not ! fifty per cent, will, frequently, have paid for seats. The Superintendent points out to me a party of fifteen - three adults and twelve children. Some of these people have also been down to the fruiting, for, one would think by a special provision of Providence, as hop farming decreases no fruit farm- ing increases, tile increasing number of hands annually required for the latter thus acting as a counterfoil to the yearly lessening deleted for hap- pickers. The " hoppers are drawn from the poorest of the east and south of London districts —the dens of Dept ford, and tire cheap lodging-houses of Bermondsey, Whitecliapel, Spitaltlelds, and Poplar. The demand for sock labour is indeed for these people a blessed thing, giving to them that boon of Providence, fresh, pure air, and currying into the miserable dens of the east end health and the happiness of bright recollections of the country in the autumn months. There are here men and women to whom this month of hop-picking is the only decently paid work obtainable during the year. "What do we do the other eleven months of the year ?" says a respectably dressed woman whom I accost. "Weil, me and the children makes match- boxes at home. Then there's lota of street hawkers comes, and even sewing girls and shirtmakers. Bless per heart, this little trip quite sets no up for the winter. Why, some of the people never seems to do anything else bat thin its all the year. You see we has a man to pull the poles out of the ground and lay them on the tresides, so we only has to pick. Me and children workin' together can strip over 50 poles a day. So we put up between in, from thirty to forty bushels a day. The pay? Well, it varies, of course. Usually a shilli lifer anything between flve anti twelve bushels, according to the crop." This, perhaps,is the reason for the regularity with which the pickers turn up at their usual place of employment. dust before the beginning of the sea- son, which, by the way, is this year unusually early, the pickers write round to the farmers, and though they are of such a roving disposition, I believe they rarely fail to acquaint their usual employer of any change in their address. Many of them, of course, have not been under the Id e-sed influence ot the School Board, and are guiltless of the scrivenic art. One man therefore will usually write letters for a dozen more. They are replied to by post-card tell- ing them when to come down, and thus, though many, of course. go "on spec." the greater number by far know exactly the garden where they may I obtain employment. Their names are entered upon the farm books, and it is interesting to note that the McCarthys and the Aliens are the oldest fami- lies who have gathered the blognom. , Sleeping accommodation is provided for them ; many of the large growers have sleeping houses, square brick buildings, each holding eight or ten persons, specially built in the gartlens. Usually, however, they occupy tents, being also provided with straw—. long feathers" the pickers call it - to sleep on, a not uncomfortable bed on. warm . ,

September night. Work commences at "nix sharp in the morning, and Ceases at the same time in the evening, a born being blown as a general signal. On leaving off there is ononhlya rush of the impecunious to the treasury, held 'by the farmer's men, where they may obtain a "cub," or advance of a shilling or soon the day's work. The wise, of course, borrow on account in this way only sufficient to purchase necessaries, with the consequence that on settling day at the end of the season they receive fit, £7, or even .ClO as the results of their efforts. But to many, usually well known at the local beer-shops, and, alas, often to the local police, this " subbing " means ruin, many of them, between the cost of liquor and the often consequent legal costs, not having suffivient money to pay their fares back again to London dirt and dreariness. The great holiday is, naturally, Sunday. On that day the picker, barbers, whom I must not forget, do a trade that can only litly be characterized as "roaring." There gentlemen not only go down to pick, but having also carried down with them a , razor or two, a shaving brush, and piece of soap, they are ready on Sunday to operate on all comers at the prices "Chin and side-wingu d.; All over" id—by no means extravagant BUMS to be paid for the removal of a week's growth of beard. Sunday is known to the pickers only an - wash- ing day.' Then the clothing, if desired, or as much

div.p: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 14, 1889.

as can be temporarily spared from the person, is washed in the nearest stream. Soap is scarce, and ones " blue-mottled" requires to be carefully watched. The country folk, indeed, who do not regard their visitors with entirely friendly feelings, e wax sarcastic over the uncleanly apparel, calling , the immigrants into their territory, 'with a truly fine irony, "the aristocracy." But the Sunday feast! On the previous night the enterprising cooler from the regions of the Borough and Whitechapel has journeyed down with the choicest of his wares, and with the delicate bloater, prime cheese at 2ted. and 3d. a pound, bacon at 3d. and 4d., and 'pieces,' (the chippings of mutton, beef, and pork from the butcher s block) at :M., the spread is indeed a treat. But here at last comes the train. Everyone col- lects his or her family and personal belongings, and, amid a babel of parting advice, last messages, and anxious inquiries, delivered in the shrillest of voices from the women, and the hoarsest of gutturals from the men, all in the dialect peculiar to eastern Lon- don, singing, shouting, whooping laughing, yes,and even with some tears, off we go for the fairyland of rural scenery. 'May Jupiter Pluvitts,or whoever else controls the elements for the present month, be propitious,and smile his brightest upon the summer holiday ot the poorest in the land, even as he is believed to smile upon the bidding of the highest- - her Majesty the goeen

'SHOCKING ASSAULT WITH A HATCHET. The Warrington magistrates, on Monday, inv.,- tigated a sermon charge of wounding. William Kylward, (30), a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with cutting and wounding his brother-in-law, Thomas Healey, of 12. Ilaydock-et., at about four o'clock on Sunday morning. The Chief-Constable (Mr. S. Hunt), informed the magistrates that the prisoner lived with the prosecutor, Thomas Healey. who is a tanner. He (the prisoner) was formerly In the Orenadier (duards. hut latterly he had been employed on the Ship Canal Works. On Sunday morning, at about four o'clock Police-Constable Jones, (29), was going along Tanners-lane, when tie • (heard

Proceeding to Ilaydock-st., he saw Mrs. Healey knocking at the doors of one or two of the neigh- bours. She then went inta the house, leaving the Idoor open, and the Constable folhwed. Ile flashed a light from his hull's eye on the scene, and was astonished to eye the prisoner, who was entirely nude, on the top of the prosecutor on the floor.

Prisoner had hold of the prosiicutor with his loft hand, I and in Nis right held a hatchet produced, which had on it. There was blood on the b.!, on the floor, and all about the place. The prisoner then jumped into bed and covered himself up, and Jones (the constable) whistled for assistance. It was unfortu- nate that they could not sentence the prisoner to more than two months imprivmment, with hard labour, which term he would have to undergo. He might have been charged with murder.—Alderman Davies ob.irvtid that the prosecutor had screened the prisoner to such an extent as would scarcely have been considered possible.

Herr Cohen is by common consent one of the cleverest exponent,/ phrenology of his day, and Into perlwps done more than any other man to bring it again within the pale of the real sciences, outside which it has passed through tricksters of the character reading profession. His life and work, to all except the blindly bigoted, are full of interest. His career has not been one of dull monotony. His work has not travelled in one unchang- ing rut. His existence Iset not maintained ono dead and uninteresting level. Since it dawned upon him that man came not into the world merely to eat, drink, and be rf7r7t: igilto9,lif.eZikt,litasloattlaitstndheTtelltywo"rfki'tourPwZch In an has put his nand, IS one of credit to the man and of benefit to the communities among which he labours. In . his day he has had to encounter the opposition of per- . sons iff high degree in every town in which he vontured to tell the people plain and oftenunpalatable truths about their habits, manners, modes of living, and of dress. .Xrniaanwhnnahiao

, in spite of obstacles arid over the heads of leon energetic and able competitors in the race is without his oppo• ! nents. But if flew Col has liii ...Met,ea they an- few and far between, for it is notorious that clergymenawl layte.en who once despised his efforts are among his most willing helpers, and that hard-headed inen in every Claw that have gone to tins lecturm to scoff have remained to pray. ((err Cohen is not noticeable on account of his personal appearance, though that is striking enough, no much as for those qualities that At him for public life, lie liana remarkable individuality. He has not only a wonderful facility of speech, but he possesses a rare fund of humour, and has a marvellous insight tucharacter and the Mothes wiliell govern the !Malan mind. Added to this he is a fearless exponent of everything that Ilia experience tells hint in wrong. Ili! never hesitates to inform his audienms of Inns opiniono on the practices of the age which drives young men to the dogs, young women to liVez, of shame. and make parents fathers and mothers in nothing but name. He is besides 0 sworn Mein,: to all shams. Atkiut so eminently useful a life as that of ileer (Alen there is a ! charm and 0 fascination that few peoplecan resist. What ! Ben Colon's pnisent exalted position is everybody in i Blackburn knows, but the steps by which he has risen, the reason which operated in Ins mind and gave bent to his character, strugglm and triumphs, are not so generally understood. It may be interesting then if we take

' and let him see the man as he is, analyse his character as I he mrkons up the intellectual value, the moral worth, and the aptitude of his clients, and reveal to them the principles which have animated him far the last 18 years. Withthis end in view ORO of our representatives has had an interview with Ilerr Cohen to glean some- t thing of the ups and downs, the discreuragements and I eneourag 1111 l ents.erf his even. ful carser. With the or- dinary- civilities eschangtekl, the •• Express " man ripened j the bat. As your name and appearance imply, you are not an Englishman, if course? Oh dear, no. I wAs horn in Prussia. I lout care to think how long ago, although I am still what might be called a young man. Have you been in this country long ? Off and en her 18 years. You speak English fluently enough now, hut you must have had difficulties with the language? I Ycs, but never great oiler. Fortunately for me, Hearn I a language very quickly. Before I set foot in England I j was master of the Hebrew, the German, the Polish, and the Hussian languages, and had a knowledge of French I and Latin. What object had yrai in view When I j landed in Hull I was making my way to Birmingham, I where Shred relatives, and the only English word S knew then was "'mud." At that time had the reading of character any fascination for you? YI'S, even as a lad. What gave an impulse to 11. studies in human nature, was a belief amongst supiCrstitior, Jew, that witches have a peculiar animal in their eves, and that if you hark closely and ffitentle you will ;ere it. And you began to he* for the animal ? I did, and though I never found it, I discover,' that there were many iteople who could not look me in the face. Following men and women ref this description at, to the crowds, I soon discovered that they were the folk whir WOUld pilfer, steal, and pick- pocket. By that simple method. I became quite an expert in l ..... "

On arrival m England did you begin immediately to continue your olnervations ? Not systematically. For a few years I drifted in the stream of popular pleasures and worldly ways. Until the nobler part of your losing was aroused as suddenly, perhaps, no with Martin Luther when he resolved to dedicate hunself to God's service iron the shock consequent on seeing one of his friends struck dead by lightning? Exactly. I WWI beginning to fool the effects, physiod and suentalsof the terrific pace at *hie), the world wags. My health was below par. I consulted no fewer than SPY.'s physicians in Nottingham, s /Idiom, and elsewhere, and, although they all tokl toe a different tale, they agreed in the main that there 'NM something serisonly wrong. Did you find rebel? Yes, lost not in the preseriptlons of the physicians. While in a distressed state of booty and mind besouse of what they had told as, I happened to notice that Prof. Fowler, the great phrenologist, was in Nottingham. I went to him and he tdd me mons in five minutes, and was snore cornet in his conclusions about soy condition, both physical and mental, than all the seven learned physicians put together. I suppssse it U"..1 then you received the inspiration which ultimately resulted in : your adoption of a public career? Yes. I was astonished 110 less than startled by what Prof. Fouler told me. That visit then may be said to have decided your future It slid. I was so hopremed wills the power this simple student of phrenology and physiology po.v.ed its benefit a young man in deapair that I deter- mined to take up the double study and do for others: what Ise had done for me. You did not at once enter upon public life Not for several years. I atolied as an amateur, and the toosion for phrenology and kindred sciences as grew upon me that I began to neglect every- thing else, M loge did you make your first plunge? At King's Lynn befora—five people ! I gathered them round the fire. I told them it was

but that I meant, whatever oltstaalm and diaeourage. manta I might meet with, to follow out the plans I had mapped nut for myself. I did then what I had not done before and have mver done vine—lexamined the heads . . . .

of all my audience! But small beginnings have some.: . tinny large endings.flerr C,d,ea ? Well, I have reason 'to be more than satisfied with the sneerou which has everywhere aitendeil my efforts, and if I began with five persons at King's Lens,! filled the largest building in the town before my visit ended. On what lines bad von concluded to work ? Well, you use though a Jew, I bail already become a Christian, and was moreover a total abstainer. My programme is and always has been one of" Practical Christianity," and with these virtues on . .•

, my side to begin with it was an easy to practise as to preach. I simply wanted to show the people the light I had received through Christ and from theact of SI 11)111 ty. I do not believe either in broken-kneed Christianity or broken-kneed teetotalism. I want everything to emanate from the individual. Wilt individual salvation . . .

risely. I have not been to Scotland' for example. I ! have visited Canada and refused invitations to Australia. Of Lancashire and Yorkshire I know every inch. I have tilletl

div.p: THU. LAIDINNT BUILDINGS IN ENO LAND,

sueli as St. James's Hall, in Manchester, the Albert Hall in Sheffield, St. iieorgco in Bradford, to leave nut of mention your own Exchange Hall, in Blackburn, and others further afield, not for a night, but nightly for weeks in succession. It stands to reason that many celebrated Ira is have come under your fingers in the last righteen years With your growing reputation? I have examined niany public characters. I spent two hours svnii John Bright before his last and fatal Wilms. I have been with Mr. tiladstame at Ilawarden, and herost his death had the pleasure of a call from the Rev. Henry Ward &vale, One hears a good deal just now of your Electric-inasoge Health Mission. Was that a , natural development of the work you had in hand ? In every sense. Coming in contact with so many men and women of every type, I found a great deal of sickness and physical defects caused by the ignorance of the laws of nature and the construction of the human body. Most of them had taken physic until they were tired. I began to study whether there was anything that would cure this modem nervous malady and what. I studied electricity pure and simple, and the application of it in a practical way. I derived my inspiration from John Wesley, Whit was the most advanced medical electrician thae we have any record of, and I invented what I call.
THE MEDICAL COIL nArrsev."

Arid you found it ever thingyou had desired ? More. I have heen amused at the marvellous power of electricity as manifested through the Coil Battery. But Fou say nothing, Ikrr Cohen, of the treatment you are givlng free of charge? That is a matter I have no desire to brag about, but it is a fact all the same that I treat 500 poor people at nil, rooms at stated hours Avery week. lain no convinced of the curative power of electricityproperly applied, that I would like V we an electric establishment provided by the ratepayers in every town, just as in the large towns there are public baths. It goes without say- ing that you have received many expressions of public approval of your work ? I have lived down the pre- judice of my early slays entirely. Yes, if you were at my rooms in Manchester I could show you 32 illumin- ated addresses I have reeeived in Lancashire, Yorkshire, and the Midland Ccuaties alone. In another respectalso, and this let use add in conclusion, I am reaping the reward of my labours. The publication of" Journal,- has, by reason of the favour with which it is ' received given use much encouragement, but what to my mind is better still, is that people clone to me nearly every day to thank me for the help I woo shit, to render them when they were at a 10.4 what to do with their sons, and to express their gratitude At the success attending them in the pursuits I indicated as likely to call their tr-st faculties into play, in many Gsses after they ha‘l signally failed in some occupation to which they had been thoughtlessly put by their parents.

Australia will be sending us a champion giant soon. A little wearenod Scotchman. named Mdasan, was resently summoned to appear beton, a Victoria provincial court for not sending his boy to school the statutory number of days. He came into court with a colossal youth by Isis side. This is the child, your worship," he reinarknl,amidst much merriment. "liquid gracious," earldom' the magistrates," what height is he ?" , feet six inches," nsplied the diminutive sweat. "And what's his age ?" " Thirteen years and nine months." • '• Well," said the magistrate. " according to his age he conies under the Education Act, though sot according to I Isis stature, so I most impose a fine of 55." The boy is described no well built, apparently healthy, and giving every promise of lusting the record of modern giants.

ALPINE ACCIDENT TO A ST. HELENS I CLERGYMAN. The Rev. J. Farnworth Anderson, recently appointed curate of the Parish Church, St. Helens, , has met with a serious accident whilst in the Alps, Switzerland. It appears that the rev. gentleman ' was spending a part of his vacation at the Riffel Alps, Zermatt, where he met the Dean of Norwich, who invited him to join in several expeditions which he organised, and which comprised a large number of ladies as well as gentlemen. Mr. Anderson enjoyed them all, and wasquite equal to any exertion which they required. Ile left the Dean and the Riffel Alp in Friday evening last, slept at Zermatt. and went down the valley to Viege, there to take the train homewards. When near Viege Cr Visp, hich is about twenty-eight orthirty mil. front Zermatt, he saw a short cut, as he supposed, and pni.eded to take it. He had taken but a few steps, when ssnm Italian 111VVieg, working on the new railway, up the valley. called him togs back, but he had gone at such a speed sod the place was so steep that he eould not retrace his steps, and he was plunged downs pre- cipice on to the rocks below. The w:rkmen made their way to him, and placed Mtn on a track, he being in great pain. Ile had broken the thigh bone of his right leg. The agony was increased by the truck running off the linao and by the efforts of the navvies to get him along. A mule was then put to the truck and he was 1 drawn along the line until slitter was procured, when 1 Is' was conveyed to the Hotel de la Poste, Visp, where he now lies. Inn few hours four Swiss surgeons were on the spot, and the leg woo set,eneased in plaster of Paris. and everything that could be done was done. Mr. Ander- son had, as may be supposed. a bad night on Saturday and on Sunday, but there is neither inflammation nor , fever, nor unfassiorable symptoms of any kind. Intel- , ligen. of the accident did not reach the Eiffel Alp till late on Monday night. The Dean of Norwich started a , little after daybreak en Tuesday, and stayed with Mr. Anderson until Liverpool friendsarrived. There is every . hope that in a few weeks hewill be able toproceed home. Natural, the accident to the Rev. Mr. An.Drson has „ occasioned much regret among his new parishioners. According to arrangements lie should have teen in St. Helens to assist in the services at the Parish Church last Sonday. The Nev. E. V. Eyeranl had cone to Dover on . his holidays, and the vicar was left to read the lessons and conduct the whole of the services. The unfortunate ' gentleman's duties were to assist at the work in Hie Parish Church, the York-st. Mission, and the Winter -„ Mission at Windle Smithies.

• Bases. the flaming gns.lamps in Ite,an -gnat, late one May night, a woman stood watehing the strati, faces passing by. She was well and nosily deemed, a lady in appearance and manner. Nevertheless, there she stood, forlont and Ministate, beneath the lamps. Many and various were the people who humid or strolled by her she regarded them all with a lidltus eye, until one passed with a quii•k, sharp step the step of a man with a purpose at heart. Iler listleia eye gathered brightness ; she looked sharply, eagerly, at him, and then followed him fol- lowed him until he turned into a quiet street, lending out from Oxford-street, and Om she closed up to his side and spoke. "Sir, you are an Ingestre?" He turned upon her in an instant with— " And how do you know that, pray "Y. u have the Ingestre head and shoulders (I should know them and the Ingestse eve bail and bright as a hawk's as savage, too. If I had met you in the Arabian Desert instead of here, I should have known you for one of their rave." "True enough ;I am Ingram Was Ingestre. What do you want with me?" 4 Cif you, rather clarity!' "Charity ! good heavens! and I am all hut beggar," he laughed scornfully. "Muir - I think I have a halfpenny in my pocket ; shall I nsult you by I offering it ?" "Put by your money, Mr. Ingram Ingo:ire." she returned, gently thrusting back his outstretched hand with the coin in it. "Money will scarcely help liii. M my strait. In this great city lam all alone. I have neither friend nor acquaintance here; I ani willing to work I want a home. Tell me, for Heaven's mke, whore I mu had a respectable one.' .• Who and what are you, my good soul? and what is it you know almut the Ingestres?" "I know, or rather knew, Ge.frge Hogs, of Redfern, many years ago. I lived as lady's-maid to his wife until I married. I have been abroad sites, then in different services, and only jost come holm+ to an old neither, whom I had dad two years ago. Now, I have wither friends nor home. My ruin" is Kedah Fanner ; and what I want now is to find a situation on housskeeper, or lady"s-maid, in same respectable ,i-r'on's family. I knew you instantly for an Ingestre, and that emboldened me to speak." Ingram Ingestre had net his teeth while she was

speirCing. - "And so you know that scoundrel at Redfern- - that thief - that- -- Ah but that is nothing to do with you. Are you telling me a parcel of lies?" "Truth, sir —truth, as I live." " You don't look like a liar. See, here is my address; if you are not an impostor. I shall expect you to-morrow evening at six o'clock. I will then till you if I ran do anything for you.- ' " I will come, Mr. Ingestre, never fear. Sir, I thank you, from my heart,' and she curtsied moot graciifully to him as she mid it. ".t very well-mannered lady's-maid,' he thoughts walking on, as a sort of excuse to himself for lifting his hat to her as she went away. "I like the Wok of her I think she will do well for poo Anna. And SO xlii knows George Ross, curse him'" Ile walked for ten minutia after that, and at last entered one of a row of houses in a wide, dull steers. It was n street of bygone grandeur, of faded and past gentility, and the great house In. went into bore iivi dew vs et the mme nature. It had fifty years before been a nobleman's now it was let out in flistre to .y one who could afford to pay twelve shillings a we ik for the accommodation. And at the top of Gm handsome old oak staircase --the very top stall Ingram Rms Ingestre. Esq., had two rooms, one for himself, and roe for lii, idiot sister. He did wrong to curse a follow-creature; he did worse in coveting what was not his owl, and hunting like a lamdliound for the vengeanee he thirsted after; but in one corner of his hard, embittensl heort he had a soft and kindly spot--n noble aod unselfish devotion to this idiot sister. wretched creature she was indeed, as she But mouthing and grinning en a stool close to the fire- place, never even lifting her lack-Imtre eyes at his entrance. She was a woman of actron or eight-and- twenty. with Lill', hands, neck, and arms hideously scarred and siamed. Her singisl-looking hair hung about her face, her dress was disorderly and not over clean, and her attitude was that of a child, as she picked sonic paper to pieces that lay seattered round

. _ her. was Anna Ingstre, the only sister of Ingram }ices, tenderly and reverently loved and cared for by him, miserable object that she was. He went upend kissed her scarred tam, took the paper from ha fingers, and asktel her if she was hungry. Ves," was the ravenous reply; .1 want my supper• She afraid have it, he said; and he went ton cup- beard, and cut her a huge slice of cake. She started up and snatched it from his hand, with the devouring greed of a wild beast. TI en she crouched down at his side to eat, with eyes fixed on the giver of the I food. ' • '

Patiently and kindly he watched her repulsive movements. and then. drawing or to a seat near him, asked what she had been doing all thu long time he had left her that day. She turned her vacant eyes on him with a sort of glimmering archness, ' ' '

"And slot do yon go for, brother. eh ?" "I go to teach music, Anna, you know; the beauti- ful music you used to bear in ehurch once upon time, when you were a little girl." e Lam a little girl now; only I have no one to dress roe. I ',IA, brother, you would let my servant dress me," she said, pettishly. "I candot remember to dress myself ! I want my nurse to dress me.' And she began to whimper. "And you shall have a servant, Anna, to drew you to-morrow. I have 4 new pupil teday, and I can afford to keep some one to look after you now. I will get you a nurse, Anna, dwr." But lwr thoughts had travelled far from that sub- ject, and her fingers were busy with some paper the had picked up from the ground. ' "1 have seen the devil today, broths.; and he gave me thin paper to play with:' ! "Oh, ; not the devil, Anna.. . . . . . . . .

"A black man, though; with white teeth, and black beard, and black hair, and black eyes. It was the devil. I knew him. Be wanted you. brother. Be said he had eonse for you. Then he gave tne this pretty paper, but not to play with. No, he put it behind the thing up there ; but / watched him, and when he was gone I got it for myself. ! hsl "and she laughed gleefully. Ingram looked closely at the paper on the ground. It had been a letter, without doubt ; but scarce a word was to be deciphered now, for it was torn into the minutest shreds. One he saw, and that was Redfern.. lie went dovnbstairs, and made inquiries whether any stranger had been into his rooms that day. No one could tell, save a small of five yeses, who thought she had heard a mauls footsteps ascentling in the morning. Ingrano went back uneasy at heart— information concerning Redfern lest to him perhaps for ever. Avid who could have brought it? Who chat he knew an.swered to his sister's description? We one. Ile questiened her gently and carefully, but she never varied frem her declaration that the deed had been there and le.h. some paper. "Yea, she knew it was. She, saw his eyes"

IMPENDING SIii7LENI ENT.

Reports were current on Saturday aftern...n, that the London dock strike had tenninatetl, but these re pnivod premature, the intelligence having been circula- ted Dimwit a misapprehension. The strike continues, the men through their Committees and leaders having rejeeted the offer of the Dock Company that the dock labourers' wages be raised from sd. to 6,1 per hour on and after Ist January nest, provided all riverside and dockmen returned to work on Monday morning. It was runieured, on Thunulay night, that it compromise had been effectisl, the men to go to work at once, and the advance to commenco on November 6th.
MANIFESTO BY. THE-.4I7IaERS.

In a mafesto issned shortly before midnight, on Saturday, the Strike Committee say. the men are not in- elintil to grant to the Dock Compames who have opposed them terms more favourable to the masters than those which have been agreed to by the wharfingers. They are willing to return to work- for any wharf, or dock, or shipping company whose representatives will sign and forward to the Strike Committee an agreement to give the terms acceded to by this wharfingers, ineluding a minimum wage of sixpence per hour ordinary time and eightpence an hour overtime. DEMONSTRATION IN HYDE PARK.

On Sunday the labourers had a demonstration in Hyde Park, where meetings were addressed tnim four plat- forms. Mr. John Bums delivered address,: at two of the mivtings, in the I•ourse of which he said that they would fight the directors as fiercely as ever, and thst arrangements had been made for another three week's strike if that should he found necessoy. Resolutions were passed unanimously pledging support to the striker, and to boll out until their moderate demands were conceded. TIIE MANSION HOUSE CONFERENCE. _ . .

The Lord Mayneg Committee considering the dock labourers strike, consisting of the Bishop of London, Carel.] Manning, Sir John Lubbock, Sir Andrew Lusk, and Mr. Sydney Buxton, resumed negotiations at the Mansion HOUK' at noon an Monday between the net and the dark directors. Mr. Norwood rioted the NUR- AIM More. on Monday afternoon, and had a short inter- view with ilk Lordship's committee. _ MEEI ING OF FIRI ERN.

Speaking at the usual meeting on Tower Hill, on Mon- day morning, Mr. Burns announced that several more wharfincers had accepted the men's terms that morning. The strike fund had received £1,500, ineluding £l.OOO from Australia. Ile denied the statement of the Lord Mayor that he and Mr Tillett had accepted the first of January compromise, and said they merely promised to lay the proposal toter the men. fie denied that he had , been guilty of a breach of faith. ....—.. . .. .

The men'a terms have now beenconceded an 37 wharves and granaries. an well as by 13 tea wharfingers. In a report to the Press on Monday morning, the dock if ins. tors said they hail made all the concession they could. There is still inactivity at the London Pocks.- A few more men were got in on Tuesday morning, but they are very few. The stevedores Will hold out. About eight hundred more men were engaged by tin wharfingers on Tuesday, on the rneres terms.
The Xntount collected throughout Victoria in aid of the London strikes is now £lO,OOO, anti in New South Wales £4,000.

iitS;teamship owners met on Tuesday. in Leadenhall- at.. but adjourned pending the receipt of a further eon.- munieation front the Dtkik Company. Sir Henry Le Marehant, one of the dock directors. has resigned be- canoe the direet. irs did not reject the Lord Mayor's pro- posals. A meeting of the strikers was held on Tuesday afternoon, outside the West India Docks. when Mr. Hums took a show of hands on the quektion whether they would aempt November Ist for the cornea ion of their terms, and they:‘,ll!!rimr!Tilytiveided_against it.

lAn exciting scene took place at Fenchurch-street Station shortly before noon on Tuesday. flinty' black- legs " on their way to the docks were followed to the railway station boa crowd, Superintendent Foster guarding the dockers with a force of police. On reach- ing the barrier on the departure platform, several men made a rush, but were prevented from getting through. Returning into the street, those who had followed the " blacklegs " vented their feelings of disappointment by : hooting and using expressions very disparaging to the character and working abilities of tlmse who departed. Earlier in the morning a body of forty " blacklegs' went by the Great Eastern from Fenchurch-street to the docks.

PROPOSED TERMS OF SETTLEMENT. Cardinal Manning's suggested compromise that the new terms should begin early in November, was dis- CUSSed, on Wednesday, with considerable eagerness by the men, and though little woo actually accomplished towards ending the strike, there stwmed to be a more confident hope among the dock labourets that the long strugale was nearly ever. At the rower Hill meeting, Mr. Tillett announced the receipt of a further sum of £4,000, from Australia. Mr. Champion maintained that the men had obtained all the concessions they had de- manded with regard to wages, and asserted that the flock Dim-tors were simply haggling as to the time at which the advance oho 41111 be given. For the tnen's own sake, however, he trotted that if they could now see a may out of the difficulty they would not hesitate to adopt it. Several other whartingers signed the agree- ment, on Wednesday, with the result that 800 additional men were engaged at the wharves. At a meeting of Congregational ministers, in London, on Wednesday, wordial sympathy woo exprpssed with the dock labourers in their struggle, the belief being also expressed that their claim was subs antially just and reasonable. CONFERENCE WITII THE DIRECTORS. On Thursday. the Dock Directors had little no say to the Press, except that it was not merely a large sun) of money that was involvwl, but that a considerable time would be requited in which to perfect the arrangements hor paying the increased wages. Great interest was taken in the conlerence between Cardinal Manning and the Directors in the afternwm, as it was expected that the meeting would he pnsluetive of beneficial re- sults. The Cardinal's mission on behalf of the men was to, a.scertain from tlie Dock Dinstors whether they wonbl he inclined too make any further roncession with regard to the time. While the Car- dinal was not altogether empowered to proms,. the 4th November as the date, it was pretty well imilerstood that the men would agree to resulne work then on the new terms. The conference steol two Imurs. The Directors considered tliat the terms they had agreed upon—to pay the higher wages front the Ist of January —were the only terms they could abide by. If the leaders of the strike had any other terms to suggest to the Directors it was for them first to, agree amongst themselves, oin,l then to submit their prontwals to the I companies. Coming. as those proposals would, through Cardinal Manning, the Directors would consider them. A telegram from London at midnight statisl that the efforts of Cardinal Manning and the Conciliation Cam'l mittee had been successful.

Mr. Donau)», one of the members. brought the question of the meat supply of the Workhouse under discussion. fie did not think it was desirable that the Guardians should invite tenders for separate supplies for officers and ! inmates. The butcher who contracted ought to I supply the meat in quarters or sides, and if there was not a joint in the quarter of the side good enough for the officers he (Mr. Dobson) maintained that the rest of the meat would not be good enough for the paupers. Mr. J. HOUGHTON said the meat used to be supplied in the way suggested by Mr. Dobson but it WRA not considered satisfactory, and the CLER K added that Mr. Dobson was proposing to go back to the system which the Board for some reasons or other decided to change. Mr. Doming explained that he did not want special quotations for officer's j ts. Camettos said that sorely Mr. Dobson liii not contend that there shoold be no differ..., betynwn the food of the officers anti that .ff the inmates. Mr. banana, That is nett iny resolution at all. PiLddrost. and its immoodiate neighbourirosl is essen- tially a poor district, but the people residing there are mostly hard-working folks. It is singularly free Irma the unfortunate class of women who infest the courts and alleys of Whitechapel. The place is wretchedly lighted, and the many little dark passages alvout make it like a rabbit warren and peculiarly easy for a criminal to slip away undetectol. Although the police authorities have made most active investigations nothing was gleaned on Weolnesday to elucidate the Pinchin-street mystery. Or. alld his assistants were occupied during the early part of the dav in carefully examining the remains and preparing an exhaustive met-that report upon the affair. They decline, however, to state anything concerning the case until tha resumed inquest ton the 24th inst. Up to the present the search for the missing portions of the body has not resulted in obtaining even a clue to work upon. Without the disrovery of the head identification is rot- : dered extremely difficult, as there are no distinctive marks or peculiaritim upon the trunk. In previous cases of this sort in Whiteehapel the clothing has gener- ally atfordoxl a clue to identity, but the police are not ! similarly aided in the prment instance. On Wednesday I Moperintendent Arnold and Inspector Reid were informed I of some chalk writing on a wall at the corner of Frederick-st ~ a dark passage in inunoliate proximity to the scene tot the discovery. Übe name of Joe Cleary was introduced with fine or six other words written OH the wall, and this being the name given by a man who made some communication about a murder to a newspaper ton Sunday morning, the coincidence attracted attention. The pollee do not, however, consider it a matter of much importance. Several persons have applied to the police for permission to view the remains, but only those who could give a reason:thief...4o were allowed to do an.

THE INQUEST. Mr. Wynne E. Rueter on Wisinesday morning opened the inquest at the Vestry Hall, Cable-nt. The first wit- ness was P.C. William Pennett. He stated that he went on duty at ten o'clock on Monday night, and was on the regular brat passing through Pinchin-st. every half-hour. It was about 5-25 when he discovered the body. He was on the northern side of Pinchinst. when he saw the body. He always looked in the arch when ressing: The body was about fire yards inside the archway, lying near the wall of the arch. The body was naked. with the excep- tion of some pieces of rag lying on it. There WiTe no marks of blood upon the ground, which was very dusty. He called a passer-by, anil sent for assistance. Two more constables came running almost iminerliatoly to the spot. Inspector Ilinborn arrived shortly after and dinyted the arches to be se:trolled. Two 1111% having the appearance of sailors, werefound asleep in one of the arches, and a shoeblack was discovered in another. ! There was nothing in the archway when he passed shortly before fio. He did not see anyone about with a costermonger's barrow or cart in Pincliinst. He was on the heat for the first tinni.—lnspector Tinhorn, the next ! witness, gave evidenee as to searching the neighbour- hood for more remains. The men taken to the station gave satisfactory accounts of theinsilves. They !mad no noise dining the night.—The Coroner adjourned the inquiry until Tuesday, the 24111 inst.

LOSS OF OVER 100 LIVES.

ANTWERP. Fattav EvENTNO.—A terrible expliion took place to-day in the livnamite Factory at AnstruweeLnear this city. Already eight corpses and 50 wounded have been brought into Antwerp. A correspondent at Antwerp writes —The authorities Seem anxious greatly to understate the number of killed and wounded, and the exact figures cannot there- fore be aseertained. The official report gives them as follows :—Killed, 106; wounded, 79 ; but the search for human remains is lit 3et completed, and mane people are supposed to have been blown into the Scheldt. Large crowds from all parts Hocked into the town on Monday to view the ruins. Sulaseriptions are being raised on all sides for the benefit of the wounilml and destitute. The inhabitants have expreased their thanks to Queen Victoria timber sympathy. DESCRIPTION BY AN EYE WITNESS.

~,,, ....... A Berlin correspomdent telegraphs the following An eye-witness of the disaster at Antwerp has given the following accoont of the fearful sconeshe saw. He said: t• The first thing I stw was a group of men carrying away the wounded. Tho ground was covered with mutilated fragments. On one side lay a hand, a foot, mrl a leg: on the other an ear, with part if the skin of the head ; not far off a whole BoaL oinol between all this people were hurrying hither and thither packing into sacks and carrying off these remains. They had filled a four-wheeled van no full of human flesh thatthree men had to lean against the do's,' to close it. Then it was drawn away by eight strong men. It was not pow- ! noble for me to remain longer. I could not hoar the sight. I returned the same way I had cone through the missal of wailing women who were tearing Bair hair in despair. In the [morgue were lying 32 unrerogn6sl bodies, and several sacks in Willett there are parts of the nomains of about twenty persons.Thr persons killed number 125, and 200 others have been injured. A judicial investigation has been opened, with the object od ascertaining who is responsible for the : catastrophe. Later telegrams have been received by the o Burgioniaster from the King and Queen expressing Mogen sympathy with the injured and the faillihr, of the vie- tuns. fir whoomsolscription lists have Nam opened in the newspapers. The shock of the explosion was no gnat that it was foqt at a distanceof 15 miles, prod.- : ing an etfeet similar to that of an earthquake. The fire had been entirely nabbed. The King, accompanied by M. Devolder, Minister of the Interior and of Public Instruction, and several other State officials, arrived at Antwo:rp on sunday afternsm, and visited the two hospi- tals where the injured are lying. His Majosty, who was loudly cheered by the people, both at the railway station alai in the streets, returned to Brussels at a quartespast five.
TERRIBLE FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN
STATION. KILLED BY AN EXPRES.q.

Happily such a shocking occurrence as that which was witnessed at Earlestown station, on Tuesday forenoon is extremely ram. On that day Joseph Andrews a highly-respected resident of Earlestown, whilst crossing the lines from one I platform to the other. was struck by a passing ex- press train. His hotly was terribly mutilated and his lifeless remains were picked up some yank away mom the spot where he was caught. Consider- ing the vast amount of passenger and good frank at Earlestown station, the frequent changes from one platform to another necessitated by the import- ance of the junction, the adjoining waggon works of the company and the colliery sidings, with the continual passing toxin fro of some of the fastest express train in the kingdom, the railway officials, from Mr. Young, the station-master, downwards, are to be congratidated on the case and the fore- thought they have exercised, which have hitherto I secured an immunity from ouch a frightful accident as that which occasioned a painful sensation in the ! district and attracted • crow 6of some hundreds of cersonto the vicinity of the railway station on The unfortunate man, Joseph Andrews, was a wheel- wright employed at the Viaduct wagon works of the L. and N. W. Railway Company, and resided with his wife :it 117, Earlestreet. He was 65 years of age, and not feeling well after a three days holiday at Black- pool, he did nit return to Ilk work on Tuesday morn. mg. He lir:reeled to the station for the purpose of visiting his brother, who lives at Atherton, and at the station prorneded to cross the line 117 tile level crossing at the Liverpool end if the pl mi atfor , nstead °fusing the tar-bridge from one platform to another. The enissing I referred to is providetl for the purpose of conveying luggage or harrows across the line, and a notice is also posted in a prominent position warning passengers not to cross the line except by the bridge. However, just at the time Andrews was leisurely crossing, a goods train was shunting, in the station on the Warrington line,and the express leaving Manchester at 10 15 was also duo to pass through. Andrews was warned of his danger by a man noised Boyle, who stood on the plat fonn, but he either did not hear him or paid no heed to it, and when , he seemed to hesitate and stand on the outside rail of the crossing, the express was heard coming along at a terrific sliest On entering the station, the driver of the express,a man named Alfred Godysonof Manchester, observed the tom standing on the rails, and immedia. tely opened his whistle, which he continued sounding far nearly 200 yards, hut the unfortunate man seemed to have kis attention taken up with the goofs train. Mr. ! Young, the stationmaster, and Mn. F. Glover, inspector i from the Wagon Works, were on the platform, and shouted to Andrews to get out of the way, hut lie paid no attention to their warnings, or to the whistling of the express. The driver of the express shut off steam, hilt WAS unable to redurn the speed in any appreciable ' degree, the result tring that the buffer of the engine struck Andrews with tremendous force on the left side, his head coming in contact with the buffer ' plan, Ti..' force of the conenssion threw him several yards away, off the line, and out of ft to way eif the train. Mr. Young, the stathm master, and Mr. J. Rothwell, ticket collislor, and a shunter named Nichols, hurried to the spot and found the man was quite dead, his head being frightfully smashed and his brains seattered about the line. Ile was picked up and earned on to the plat- form, and after the 'rile, had been advised, the tasty was taken home on the ambulance litter. P.C. Bowes accompanied the body home, and had it stripped, when it was found that besides the injury to the head, the body had been mangled almost out of all shape and pre singed a fearful spectacle. The tmin which was eon-1 sorted with the accident was the exprms which leaves' Manchester at 10.15, and aceomplishes the journey to Liverpool, a distance of about 35 miles, in 40 minutes, and when passing Earlestown would be travelling at full speed. The driver as nom salts saw the accident applied the vacuum brake,and alsone steam brake on the engine, which was the means of bring the train to a stop some distance from the station and atria five minutes later resumed the journey. Thorns-easel leaves a widow and a gniwn up family, all of when are married. He had heel in the employ of the Railway Ounpany for about 20years, and appeatel to he quite sober.

THE EXAMINER, SATI)RI)AI, SEPT'EMBER 14, 1889. ANOTHER WHITECHAPEL DYNAMITE EXPLOSION NEARI REVISING THE LISTS. HORROR. ANTWERP. MUIIDER AND MUTILATION. London was startled early on Tuesday morning i by the report of another horrible murder n White- chapel- one of the long series now associated with the mysterious "Jack the Ri?per." Later informa- tion. indeed, throws considerable doubt upon this being one of the Ripper crimes, hut nevertheless it is certain that a most brutal murder has been com- mittethattended with shocking mutilations. The site of Tuesday morning's discovery is a railway arch in Pinclon-st., which in Clow to Cable-nt., and in the immediate vicinity of the other murders. This arch is one of three used by the Vestry of St. George's- in-tine-East as stone yards, although they have only employed them for this purpose for the past eight weeks. Originally they were all boanled up to a height of several feet, but in the particular arch where the remains were found the hoarding hail been taken away, presumably by the ppur of the neighbourhood for tfrewood, and I hus it Is perfectly open to the street. The arch, however, is dark, no lamplight shining into it. Just before i''s.lo on Tuesday morning Constable Pennett observed in the growing light what appeared to be a body, and on closer examination disclosed the remains of a woman. The head was absent, as were also the legs, the latter having been disjointed at the thighs. The body, which was nude and lying breast downwards, showed further mutilations, and lying on the trunk was a rent chemise, all crumpled and blood-stained. There was no blood upon the ground, however, and very little On the body, and Oh, showed very conclusively that the crime could not have been committed on the spot. Constable Pennell blew his whistle, and in a very few minutes, • ice cordon was strewn around the locality. The ▪ eareful search Was made in all the eourts and a I •vs adjoining,but the only discovery vvortin record- ing Was that of three sailors, who were asleep in an adjoining arch. These men were taken to Leman-nt. Police Station. where they were subjected to examination. Fortunately for them- selves, they were able to explain their movements, and they satisfied the police that they had nothing whatever to do with the horrible crime. They had neither seen nor heanl anything unusual during the time they were in the archway, and accordingly they Were 80On discharged. Or, Clark. representing Dr. Phillips, the police divisional surgeon, made a cursory examination of the remains very shortly alter the discovery. The deceased appears to have been between thirtv and forts- years of age, antabout five feet three inches in heiiht. The trunk measored two feet three incurs, and the arms two feet two inches. Thcre was a sharp cut as of a eord on the wrist, but this might well have been , done in the removal of the remains. The cleanness of the 1 wits and the knowledge of surgery displayed in dissect• ' ing the Imily are taken as throwing doubt upon this crime being the work of "Jack the Ripper." That fiend did all his terrible work roughly, though firmly, and without any approach to scientific knowledge. The present crime bears a closer reseinWanre to the mysterious outrages at Rainbow, on the Thames Embankment, near Whitehall, and at Rattersea,than to the terrible deeds of the White- chapel terror. In each of the foregoing cases the head of the victim was missing and the manner of muti- lationsimilar. It is most probable that the murderer took advantage of the scare produced by the East End tragedies to (lispoe of his victim in away and in such a place as should throw all suspicion opon the author of those crimes. Constable Permatt is certain that the body was not in the arellway at five o'clock, or a few minutes after, when lie passed the spot. He covers his heat in fifteen minutes, and on coming round the neat time the body was there. He saw no one Altana:lOWs during his round, nor have the police definite information yet of anyone having seen any suspicious persons carrying a such or large bundle at that early IWOe. The body was removed to the St. tienrge's Mortuary., and a large crowd gathered there, remaining thninglinut the whole day. Many women of a certain class called to see the trunk, hot none could identify it. In fact, then. are no marks whatsoever on the renlaine Which would enable anyone to conclusively identify the body. and unless some other portions are discovelid it is quite pws- , sible that the 'natter will ever reinain a mystery. The ! have no present knowledge of anyone missing corresponding with the description of the remains of the deceasisl. Daring the week Mr. James Thomas roard, barris- ter-at-law, of the Inner Temple, has gone through the somewhat tedious work of revising the lists of parliamentary vote., and of burgesses and county electors, for the borough of Warrington. The sitt- ings, which have been held in the Assembly-room at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-st., commenced on Mon- day evening, when claims and objections from all polling districts were considered. On Tuesday claims and objections were taken front the north-west, south-west, and Latchford polling districts, and on Wednesday for the north-east and south-east polling districts. During the revi- sion the Liberal party has been represented by Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, awl by Mr. J. Clayton, the Liberal registration agent, whilst the Conservative party were represented by Mr. John Ilampson, the registration agent of the Con- servative party. Amongst those who have also been present during the proceedings are Mews. J. L. Whittle (deputy town-clerk). J. L. Tuustall (assis- tant overseer for Warrington), S. Hawkins (assistant overseer for Latchford), and T. I larbourne and T. J. Garnett (relieving officers forth.. Warring- ton Union). The total number of claims made was 371, and objections Mal, and they were about equally divided between the two political parties. The revision passed off very quietly, apparently little interest being taken in the proceedings on the part of the general "att.__

Adesporate affray is reported from Newport, Tipperary, on the borders of the county Limerick. It arose out of a long-stand lispute as to a right of way acrivis the farm of a man named Egan. Some men were on Sunday evening, crossing the farm when Egan came out and no. fused them permission, although the passage was claimed to he a right of way. A tight ensued, and Egan with a hatchet decapitated one man, and dreadfully hacked another, who is not expected to recover. Egan has been arrested.

HOME RULE DEMONSTRATION AT WATERFORD. A deputation of the English Home Rule Union, con- sisting of Mr Summers, M.P., Lady Sandhurst, Mr. J. Jenkinson, and Mr. Morton, secretary, visited Waterford, on Tuesday, and were received with groat public demon- stration. At a public noting m the evening, at which the Mayor and several Nationalists members were pre- sent. Lady Sandhurst said the womanhood of England was with them. They had a hundred associations firmly established, all working for Ireland, and when Mr. : Oladstone returned to power Iniland woold get her rights. Mr. Summers said England had given Ireland ' 85 Coercion Acts, and in return, Ireland had returned 85 membirs pledged to Home Rule. Mr. T. Healy, M.P., also spoke. BOATINO DISASTEIL—FIVE LIVES LOST. div.p: THE MURDER OF A TOURIST.

-- A n4port was current in Greenock, on Monday, that Laurie, the alleged lioatfell murderer, who is at pnwent ismfined in Greenock Gaol, was to be removed to Rothe- say in the foreinsin for further examination. The rumonr caused a large number 44 lieople anxious to get a ghillies. of theaccused. to congregate in the vicinity of the prison, but after some time they were assuivd that Laurie would not he taken to kothiway that day. The prisoner, since his inearceration ii, Greenock Gaol, has been very quiet, and speaks little. He sleeps and takes his food well, and appears to find pleasure in reading the hooks supplied to ida, from the prison library. A careful watch is kept over him by the warders.

LAURIE COMMITTED FOR TRIAL. John W. Laurie. who is wooed of munlering an English tourist in Arran, was mid, examination before the Sheriff, at the Greenock Court, on Wednesday. Laurie showial remarkable lirmutss. The only symptom of excitement that he evinced was a quivering id the under lip. The wowed was pale and haggard. The proceolings were conducted in private. It is undenitood that Laurie. ailing.... the advice of his law agent, emitted a declaration the ter-Se of which has not transping. When under examination it Rothe...3-, eight days ago, Laurie refused to make any statement. At the close of the examination, OM Wednsiday, he was for- mally committed for trial on the capital charge.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT OF JEWELLERY.-A
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT OF JEWELLERY.-A
STRANGE STORY.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday • morning, Clixabeth Chadwick, a young woman, • lately residing with her parents in Lord-street, Latchford, was brought up under. warrant charged • with having on or about the 2slrd August stolen a gold watch, gold necklet, gold locket, gold pencil case, and gold brooch, together value ..f7, the pro- perty of Thomas A. J. Pilkington. From a state- ment made by the Chief Countable and evidence given, it appearisl that during the absence of Mrs. Pilkington at Blackpool, the articles enumerated is the charge disappeared from the wardrobe drawer in which they had been when she left home. The loss was reported to the police, and Constable Monaghan was instructed to institute inquiries. Minnie Illagg, the servant, was subjected to exam- ination. and she stated that on the evening of the 23rd August the prisoner Chadwick came to the house. Chadwick's father was employed by Mr. l'ilkington, seno but the prosecutor pabl him his Wag. : and on the evening named the prisoner tVII.B sent by her father for his ages. Mr. l'ilkington was out at the time, and being invited by Blagg to wait, prisoner did ant. Blagg went into the cellar and remained there about ten minutes chopping wood. On returning she was stirpri,ed to see the prisoner on the stairs, coining 11,,W11 from the bed- rooms. Prisoner went very red in the face on being caught, but the servant, acconling to her own account, said nothing to her, although prisoner had previously inquired where Mrs. Pilkington put her jewellery and been told by Blagg. Prisoner after- wards left, bra called again on the following Mon- day for the Wage. It VMS the prosecutors little son who first discovered the loss of the articles. 'cone of the missing jewellery had been recoverrn. l'risoner strongly asserted her innocence of the charge preferrrn against her, saying that she hail seen nothing of the missing jewellery, and that she did not go near the stairs. The Chairman Raid that the Bench had rem, to the conclusion that there was no case against the prirnner, and that if the things were gone suspicion pointed in another direction. The prisoner was accordingly dis- charged.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
:,ATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 14. 1889.
A generation has gone by since IT and EDWIN WAUGH took the hearts of

rigs Lammshire people by storm with •• time Whoitin to thi!der and Me." He him- self has meantime grown old -he is now in his ...eventy-third year--but he has never ceased to sing: and iii the priment year of grace we have a seeand series of •• Poems and Songs." We have dipped into this volume again and again with unfailing profit and delight sailsl, tannin; one of ' his plirastsi to apply it tsr the poet, we are tempted to exclaim -
A m 1,., ee sings so weel as this Should tielrer awse to dee.

EDWIN WAUGH is a true son of toil ; he had a hard bringing up in the hard times of sixty years ago : arid it is, therefore,with real knowledge and genuine °cling, that he lets warbled his woodnotee wild o singing the short but simple annals of the vior. But wild though his notes are, that is not to say that they an, rude and uncultured. On tint, con- trary, no one who has Inado himself familiar with WAVUH'S writings—whether in prose Or 1/01140—,:111 ail to perceive that,while nature has done so much , for him, art has had no small share in produc- ing that charm of style which is inseparable I I rom everything that proceeds from his pen. There air pretentious people who sneer at the dialect as something barbarous ; they are strangers to Ws vo ifs songs because they cannot understand them: hut let them turn , to " Besom Ben," or discriptions of the Lake Country, and if they know anything of good English they will acknowledge that they are in the Pretence of a master. And so of this second series of " Poems and Songs." The poeins are for the most part written in ordinary English, while the songs are, on the other hand, almost entirely in the dialect. WAUGH is like Brass in many respects, and in none more than in this —that, whilst he is unique and unrivalled when he uses his native Doric, his thoughts,whenever they are cast in verse, fare always cast in a truly poetic mould. Take for instance, the following from the " The Lost Shepherd," the first poem in the book :

O'er the wild ridge of Pendia The wintry winds sweep; On the lone waste of Penile The mon fall is deep : Near the bleak mountains crest. Where the sildest drifts rest, With the snow on his breast. The wanderer's asleep.
Is not this diseriptive poetry if the highest order ? We have a liner strain still in the serenade, "Good Night!" the first stanza 1.1 which is as

The sun has dipped hiA golden rim Beyond the western sea : The soft wind sings its evening hymn Unto the drowsy lea; The wild waves' surging murmurs creep Along the lonely sand ; The kiss of twilight lulls to sleep The eyelids of the land. flood night. my love, good night This.slike as to thought and expression, is so much beyond the average verse which is year by year set to music and finds its way into the dratwing-ruom that a composer of the first rank would see in it an I exceptional opportimity for the exercise of his powers. But it is in the dialect that we see Waugh at his beat ; and those who are fortunate enough to possess this new volume will 80011 eon- vinee themselves that his heart still thrills. and that his hand low lust none of its cunning. Our LNIKIIShiTO LAUREATE has a peculiar affection for the violin ; he has again and again sung the magic of " the merry bit o' timber,- but he has never been more felicitous than in the latest address "To my old fiddle.- We will ,with the poet's permission, take an early opportunity of reprint- the whole poem, and meanwhile we set the reader's mouth watering with a taste of its qualities. The Fiddler, says lie, " wouldn't swop his music-kiat to own a wint n, moire)',' and then :

. • For itean "oh, an moan an' sigh, An' it can pout an' whimper: An' it can coax an whee.lle sly, An it can lisp ami simper ; An it can laugh, an' crow an' shout, An' it can wail so keen, oh. Folk cannot see their gate about For th' wayter i' their e'en, oh !

We have not left ourselves space for more than another quotation or two. Here is an extract from " Toothsome Advice" -a title which, it will he seen, is Iminourously appropriate. " Owd Mary," giving Nancy a hint as to managing her husband, says :--- . .
Thou mita have his meals cooked to his mind. At reet time, in daieently laid; Tilt pains; an, thou'll very soon did
How nice a plain dish can be made; Good cookin' keeps likin' alive,

With a woman that s noon short o wit; An there's never a craiter Ftle hive Burs fond of a toot Imome tit bit ! There are thousands of wives of working-men who would th, well to act on this" Toothsome Advice " they might lintl it was one way of inducing their hush:lnds to like home better than the ale-house. The " Lapstom, Song tells of a cobbler, whose wife was something of a Tartar ; and, touching Oils, we have the following characteristic stroke : I sometimes wished she was a man. Because she needed welting; Yet one kind word from my dray Nan Would net my heart a-melting.

With this we must conclude: wo-have quoted sufficient to indicate that Edwin Waugh is still merry, :mil wise, and g4““1; and that his latest volume of verse will he found to In, an evergreen -like the laurel he has so hing worn.

Typhoid Tue Runcorn Rural Sanitary Fever. Authority had before them, on Tuesday, a special report as to typhoid fever which had been prepared by Dr. Aloes, Medical Officer Of Health. It would sumo that this moist dangerous infectious disease has raw le its appear:slim in various parts of the Union. There have been cases at Weldon, Froilshatii Itridge, Seitton, and Norton : and—the report pro- ceeds -" information was also to hand of alleged cases of typhoid fever at I I alton, Kingsley. and Appleton:' There is, mu fart, an epidemic of the disease, and the residents of these districts cannot Is. too careful fla to their conduct. So far as caa be gathered, the outbreak, at Weston, was by workmen drinking impure water ; rr it was the same at Norton. It will bo seen, tore. that tiers is every need to lie- s •o• of wing w iter fri in an unusual weiros. L:.vos dutibt About W.

water it should be boiled. And so with milk, for typhoid fever may be ma 1111 l unicated by impure milk as well as impure water. It is also desirable to see to drainage, and, if there is a bad smell about the house, not to rest satisfied until the cause is found and removed. Traps for preventing the escape of sewer gas are too often traps of another kind. They sometimes get out of order —especially in dry weather—and then they Income death-traps through letting foul gas into living roonm. When fever has actually made its appearance, visitors should be rigidly excluded from seeing the patient ; for if theyhave no regard to their own lives they ought to be made to realise that they have no rigid to endanger the lives of other people. If neighbours desire to be neigh- bourly and helpful, there are many ways of rendering service without running unnecessary risk. An epidemic is like a conflagration, and it may be put out as a tire is put out —if the right means be taken. It is a matter of course to say that energetic steps require to be taken by the Medical Officer 14 Health ; and, if his advice be followed, the epidemic may be con- trolled before ninny lives are lost. It is equally a matter of course to say that the Sanitary Authority should spare neither trouble nor ex- pence in seeing to it that the humblest ratepayer is supplied with plenty of wholesome water. But this is just me of those things that is moot neglected a there are wheels within wheels—into- rests within interests—and it too frequently happens that isolated emmtry people are left, at a pinch, to help themselves to ditch water, just because, to do the right thing, the landlord or the towmhip would be put to expense. It is a serious matter—this outbreak if typhoid fever in so many townships ; and it is to be hoped that the authorities and the residents will actively co- operate in doing everything that is requisite to stamp out the disease.
The people of Scotland are showing Free Eat.„„,„,. thernrielves. wido-awake to the

nmeaLem educational advantages which the new Local Government Act confers upon them. They have obtained the proceeds of the probate , duty as a sort of extra grant in aid; and there is every nahcation already that they intend to make full use of them. Out of 230 School Boards, as many as 110 have declared in favour of Free Education in all sch4sds excepting high schools and academies ; and most of the other Boards would make education free up to Standard five. The Lord Advocate when expounding his scheme, was careful to say that the grant of the probate duty was not with intention of affording gratuitous instruction ; hut ha will find that, whilst he has been thinking of going part of the way, the people of Scotland have made up their minds to complete the journey. It is not unlikely that them will, for a time, he a considerable amount of friction between the central and the load authorities; but the local authorities are sure to have their way in the end ; for it is only a Imatter of a few thousand p.m& more to eneure that education in Scotland shall he entirely free in every standard in the elementary schools. Mean- time it is for English parents to ask themselves lhow it is that no such boon is offered to them as is , being conferred upon the Scottish. Is there no pro- bate duty in England that can be applied to edu- cation What in sauce for the Scotch goose should surely be saucefor the English gander.

Primo M igen has been writing in a Greek magazine about 'the new smokeless gunpowder." But the need of the present age is harmless gun- powder, with an international law compelling all countries to use it. We are a little way off that an yet ; but we may expect it—.
When the war-drum throbs no longer, Awl the hattle-flag is furled In the Parliament of man-- The Federation of the World.

An International (engross of Spiritualists was opened in Paris, on Tuesday, and one member announced that he "would exhibit some photo- graphs of disembodied spirits." It is very obliging of the spirits to permit themselves to Int photo- graphed ; but we cent help thinking that they would he better employ.' in r if ping out by moans of a table, or some other wooden leg, who "Jack the Ripper" is, and where he is to be found, " Business first, pleasure after."

Mr. Gladstone is h;tri—e—ag—ain, after frisking it at the Paris Exhibition. He was, of course, lionised and banquetised, and delighted Frenchmen by a capital speech in capital French. Bat that is his way, you know. When he went as British Com- missioner to deliver up the lonian Islands he spoke Greek to the Greeks ; when in Italy not long sines he twd Italian ; and whenever he crosses the Styx we icily he sure lie will chat with the ; grim ferryman in one of the " dead" languages. Mr. Chaplin is having to light for his seat as the !President if the Department of Agriculture, and it has made him thoughtful. In the address which 11 he has issued he tells the tileaford voters that "it would henna error to regard the creation of a Government DepsTtment as a remedy for !agricultural depremion. Jost £lO ; the Department is great, and the President is great; but it is as I well to let it he known that they one not the son I mai the moon, and all the little stars.

Jury-packing is still practiced in Ireland. The other day, in the ease of an influent, Counsel for the next-of-kin had to protest against the COlll- - of the jury, on which "there were seven Proteatante, while one of the Catholics had a !brother in the police form, and three of the remain- ing four gala they understood only the Irish lawn- age, and did not understand their poaition." And Ulla a Catholic section of a Catholic country! It is diagracef ii; there is no other word for it.

It transpires from later information to hand that I Mr. Firth, M.P., died not fl,llll sunstroke, but I from heart disease. He had start4sl alone to climb I the Flegere, lear Chamonnix, and was fowl(' dead just beyond n little inn on the side of the moun- tain. Assuming it was known that Mr. Firth suffered from heart disease, he ought to have been warned against such heavy exertion as mountain climbing, lint doctors, from mistaken kindnese, sometinice refrain from telling a patient how it stands with hire ; an extra strain cornea, and the result is that a valuable life is suddenly ended.

The Yankees are having some remarkable—very remarkable—bidloming :evident& Last week tlie story was of a little girl, who had been caught by a car rope, lifted into a tree, and then dropped into a lake just at the right spot to be saved by a boat- man. This week, the rope of a passing balloon has caught a boy by the neck ;he is "carried for , miles: but pmvents strangulation by thrusting , his hands between his neck and the rope, and, of course, reaches the ground uninjured. This is a very pretty story, but these balloon incidents are getting monotonous. If the Yankee " story teller doesn't strike out a new line, his occupation will be gone.
