ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT. A MARRIED COUPLE ON THE SPREE. On Thin—day. at the Warrington Borough Police I Court, a Welshman mimed James Evans. who has I been living in Warrington for a month or two, wax; charged with having committed an aggravated I issault on his wife on the previous day. A constable ' who was on duty at Friars-green heard a disturbance, and, going to the place, he saw the prisoner kicking , his wife, who was on the ground. She was insensible I and a doctor who was called in said that she was in a dangerous condition for the time being. as there might he internal bleeding. Proseentrix, who was now able to attend, said that she did not wish I t• tress the ease. She only recollected her husband giving her one blow and one kick. They had inarrelled because she had been singing in a public' house, and she had run at him with a knife. Prisoner said they had both been on the spree. lie was bound over in his own recognisant.es to be of good behavionr, and ordered to pay 10s. 041. costs. AN UNWELCOME IsoVPM A rather peculiar case was heard by the Warring- I ton magistrates on Wednesday morning. A young fellow named Henry Wilson, described as an out- I porter, was brought op in custody on a charge of having stolen a shawl. value 2.5., the property of a I young married woman named Mary France. Mr. ' Hunt (Chief Constable) said that prisoner and France formerly cohabited together, but a few months ago the latter took a husband. Prisoner had since persisted in keeping her company, and would wallet her alone. The two were drinking together on Satunlay night, and shortly before midni.,ht a constable saw them sitting on a doorstep in Mersey-st., having with them a quart bottle of beer. The woman was then wearing the shawl. About an hour afterwards the same constable passed the place again, and saw that France was alone. She was asleep, and Was not then wearing the shawl. She wan taken to the Blidewell, and complained that Wilson had taken the shawl, which was after-1 wards found at his lodgings. Prisoner, who said that France threw the shawl at him, made his 22nd appearance, and has" done six months " for assault- ing France. Ile was now Rent to prison, with hard labour, for a month. Bonevto KNOCKTON is TROCIUM AGAIEN. Bodelia Knockton. a young woman who is by this . time pretty fatniliar with Police Courts and onion, was. on Monday. brought up in custody before the Warrington magistrates, on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on Saturday night, and further on a charge of having tried to pick the pocket of a man named Cavanagh, with whom she seemed to have been in company. Con- stable Caldwell spoke to seeing the prisoner, when drank, withdrawing her hand from the vest pocket of Cavanagh, knit 09 that individual failed to attend to give evidence against her, the charge of attempt- ing to rifle him pockets Was withdrawn. Prisoner. who admitted having been drunk. remarked that the magistrates might as well send her to an asylum it once, because they had nearly driven her out of her mind by sending her to prison. No sooner was she out of goal. than she was in again. The character sheet of the prisoner showed a large number of con- victions, but the magistrates If POWItSI to give her a chance, and discharged her on receiving her pro- mise that she wonlrl be better in future. She laughed as she left the court. In connection with the same caw., a young man named James Jordan. wh is also well-known to the police, was brought up charged with drunkenness. He wan further charged with having attempted to reneue Knockton from the custody of the police, and with having assaulted Sergeant Cheney, of the police force. Ile wax fined 20e. and costs, or, in default, imprison- ment with hard labour for a month. THE ALLMORD SHOP BREAKING. THE MISER'S DIAMOND NECKLACE At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday morning, John Wilson, ethos Jones, was brought up on remand charged with having broken into the shop of Ueorge Jackson, pawnbroker, Winwick-at., in August, and stolen about £.45 worth of jewellery and other articles, under circumstances previously reported. Mary Baines, of Liverpool, was charged with having remived the property, knowing it to have been stolen. The Chief Constable said that since prisoners were last before the Court more of the stolen articles had been recovered. The police were doing their best to discover the rest, but they had a difficult job, as they had some very old hands to deal with. One or two persons supposed to be concerned in the case were in custody us Liverpool, • and he hoped that they would be remanded to War-1 rington. On the application of NI, Runt, Wilson and Baines were remanded until next Tuesday.

In the year 1740 there lived, in the Latin quarter in , Paris, a famous miser named Jean Ave., The wealth! , concealed in the obscure rockery where he resided was believed to be fabulous, and was no doubt really very great. Among his treasures was a celebrated diamond necklace of immense value. HE tot of thoso who toil from day to (lay in the bowels of the earth is not very agreeab?e one. Apart from, the terribla _ _ _ • - - - _

risks ef which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, with all its thrilting scenes, tit., collier has to pursue his work at times ander circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowlos, of i Of), Oxford Itoatl, Burnley, has had some experince of the trying conditions of labour in some ef the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had t work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the Same time Iropping all over his body from above. Happily such conlitions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to encounter them in other mining sufferer in con,:equence. He first commenced with pains in his hen,l, which gradually extended to other parts of the body.• " I ••ot so low," said Mr. Knowles, "that I was obliged to be covered with blankets and have a chair 411 y It was only then Clat I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that had to have the help Of a stick to get across the floor. I was terribly troubled with indiges- tion, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of cramp in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours together, and got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. Medicine only seemed to make me worse, and I got so that my friends gave me ii
'MTH
and the doctor ventured to offer no bope of a cure.
At-last I re 3

one of Warner's pamphlets, sent bra bottle of 'Warner's SAFE Cure,' and oh! how much good it did me. In a few weeks I was new man. My appetite returned, the weakness disappeared, and went back to my work feeling stronger than I had done for years.'

THE LANCASHIRE VOLUNTEERS AND THE HOME DEFENCE SCHEME. It has been decided by the military authorities charged with the home defence scheme that in the event of an invasion the enemy would in all pro- bability make for London. as the moat effective mei hod of breaking down internal defence, and chat the decisive engagement would most likely be fought somewhere southward or north-eastward of the metropolis. In preparation for such a crisis two linen of defence have been marked out, the one be - tiseen Guildford and Sevenoaks, and the other from Tilbury to Epping, and to these lines about 90,000 volunteers and 2.50 guns have been allotted. Tl. e volunteers selected are the mobile brigades all over the country, and all the mobile infantry volunteers of Lancashire have been detailed for Epping,with the position guns of the Snd Lancashire (Liverpool) and 7th (Manchester) Artillery Corps. The Great Mer- sey Brigade of Id battalions numbering 12,500 men from Liverpool,Bory,Rochdale, Salford,Birkenhead, Chester,Warrington, St. Ilelens,Preston,Bolton, and Oldham, would he left its a garrison to guard the important local interests,with the gunners of the lot 4th, and 81h Lancashire Artillery- all Liverpool corps. It in understood that the most p erfect arrangements have been made by the higher rail- way officials constituting the engineer ond Railway Volunteer Staff corps for the rapid transport of the Lancashire battalions and the other brigades to their places in the London line of defence ; and it is cal- culated that within three days of the order for mobilisation being given the Lancashire corps could all be delivered at their station on the North-east- ern line, which, with the four other brigades to he used, would then be held by 30,0110 infantry volun- teers, with the volunteer gunners and any avail- able regular and militia troops tao be minted in addition. Already places are being selected for entrenched camps and gun batteries, which could be speedily mode; and attention is being given to the preparation of storehouses and magazines a Government fluty while efforts will once more be made to induce volunteer commanding officers to organise their regimental transport and commissa- riat services in a manner that shall make the defence brigade more truly mobilo, than they are at present.

I have a warehouse where! keep toy hay and straw, and arn in nightly dread if a conflagration, if by chance one of these fireworks should be thrown into it. div.head: OUR NATIONAL POVERTY,-THE FARMERS' FRIENDS.
div.p: OUR NATIONAL POVERTY,-THE FARMERS' FRIENDS.

Sir,—lt is an inconvenience and frequently a loss financially to have too many friends. That is the case with the British fanner at the prewmt time ; his friends are numerous and in a friendly way they impoverish him. First, his landlord allows him to till the soil. ts My Land, mark vain," says the landlord ; .` you must find the capital and labour and use it under my directions— sad don't forget—l must have the lion's share of the produce. You must feed my hares and rabbits, and he gime you don't frighten them with your dogs. 'The Grea,a4 flame Act,' as tarot you and I are concerned, is a dead letter. Be punctual with your rent, and if you are ready on the rent day I will allow you to drink my health at your own expense," Second friend, the clergyman, whose pious ancestor hdt him a share in the bwiness—which the clergyntan and his friends have done their text to improve not by nay outlay or eaertiop of their own--exrept in the direc- tion of what they call an, than is Act of Parliament for the imprememett of tithe, making it easier to collect pounds, shillings, and pence, than live stock, each as pip, lambs, calves, germ% ducks, hr., sheaves of corn, andu of hay, pofid,,,i, and other produce which Man formerly collected in kind—hut now in coin—the cur- rent coin of the realm. He has other friends. The middleman, as third friend. Ile buys his produce at a low figure ad sells it at a high one, making 25 per cent. pmfit. Another friend is the butcher who bids him sd. a pound fir his stick, and sells the meat at 10,1. The milkman gives him 7d. a gallon for his milk, and sells It at a shilling to it. 441. on gallon. Then the Railway Companies charge him 50 per cent, more for marrying his produce than they charge the foreigner for tie -owe stuff the same distance—a...scandalous injustice and inconsistency. Well may he soy—" Save me from iny friends.'' list he does not say an—no, he grins 1 and bears it, and believes his landlord to Sr hie twist friend, and next to the clergyman who has taught him ! the" pastor and matter" theory, and that the Tory policy in the beet for him. He believes it and votes tneeordingly. Ile raves for protection, and he tennis it, but the protection that he calls for lie will never get. A duty prohibiting the importation of foreign bathe will never see. The protection he needs is the power hind himself of those friends who fatten on him—the proba- tion of combination and of ro-operation in the distri- bution nf his produce ; the protecticin of a fair rent, and a right in the soil that he holds and tills ;protection for the outlay of capital ; protection from the rapacity of railway direct,mn and managers in the carriage nf farm produce and manure. He has powerful opponents to deal with, but by energetic combination be may be as stmtg or stronger than they, and ultimately become B. vietnr.—l am, Sir, yours respectfully, hairy Bridges, Sept. - .-..-.. ...... ...... The re-count of the votes in the Runcorn Com- I missioners election has shown the first declaration to be practically correct. Mr. Timmins loses one vote, and lie and Mr. liankinson thus tie for second honours Mr. Yarwood, who threatened a scrutiny, remains where he was.

The system of voting at this election in antiqu- I ated,unsatisfactory,and altogether a disgrace to the latter end of the nineteenth century. It is not nec:ssury to nominate candidates. A ratepayer may up to the close ot the poll vote for any towns- man whom his lively fancy may select, so long as he possesses the necessary property qualifica- tion. Ile may demand a voting paper front the rettimieg officer, and till it up secretly, but the officials in the booth become acquainted with hie, intentions immediately he hands the paper in, and on a scrutiny the manner of his voting may become more widely known. The more common method is for the candidates and their henchmen to obtain a good supply of papers, till in the names of I the candidatea it iN desired that the votes shall be recorder' for, and then watch that the "free and independent " initials it according to instructions. Ills not to be wondered at, therefore, that the number of votes recorded is not very heavy. When the district councils are formed, and the ballot is introduced, a revolution will be witnessed and the candidate healing the poll will have I he good wishes of more than 529 electors,

Mr. W. Mellor and Dr. McDougall have together made niliseovery at Runcorn Cemetery that will rob the numerous visitors of the pleasure they have hitherto experienced in walking along the well kept ;• walks, and viewing the equally well kept Hower ! beds and green award. The sewer which drains the cemetery and many of the graves is said to be ven- tilated in about 40 or :50 places along the walks, and the foul fumes are allowed to escape into the air without let or hindrance. Dr. McDougall suggests that the openings should at once be trapped or the " People's Park " may become a disseminator of disease and death amongst the very numerous class who are fond of consulting the " stony records of the past " and musing on the Bhakesperian pro- blem of "To he, or not to be. 'The gardener declares there is no nuisance, and never has been, and there ia therefore no immediate cause for alarm. The Burial Board, with whose admirable management no fault can be found, will doubtless 01 once do the thing needful. .

Perhaps the cemetery will be less used as a plea- sure resort when Mr. Ilankinson has accomplished his gnind idea of a park on the Common. -"When the County Court Judge ruled that Widnes Local Board could not recover from a ratepayer of the township for the expenses of the Fire Bri- gade, a cry went up to disband the Brigade at once, and not burden the rates for the benefit of the insurance companies. Inquiry has revealed that the respectable" companies gladly pay the ex- penses of the lire brigades, and as there can he no doubt as to the great usefulness of the Widnes I Brigade, the Local Board have unanimously resolved that it should be maintained inn state of efficiency. This decision will be met with universal approval.

div.head: OrTLINES OF THEOSOPHY.
div.p: OrTLINES OF THEOSOPHY.

S—The subject of Theosophy has of late been at- tracting so much attention, that a brief sketch of some of its principal teachings may not be without interest to your readers. The materialism of to-day has entered 60 deeply into every form of religion, II at any attempt to counteract its influence, should be welcomed by all who have the best interests of religion in general at heart, and especially by those WhO, at last, are beginning to perceive that it IA something more than a mere adhe- : sion to creed and dogma, and something deeper than the formula, of the churches. Theosophy atta flms no efficacy to any creed whatever. but, holding that the spirit of every man is a direct emanation from the Divine, and is destined to reunion with its sooree, it teaches that this reunion is only to be etleeted by a persistent attrition, tending to destroy the senoe of personality which alone holds roan aloof In on his fellows. Not until lvery selfish impulse 11an bell, destroyed, not until every material longing has been finally subdued. call tiliA reunion be accomplished, and the subjection of the lower nature HMS beCOMCS the first duty id the Tbeomphist. . .

This process of subjection and porifieation cannot, however, be einupletesi in one earth life. At the deathof the Isidy, the spirit enters into a condition of subjective existence where it absorbs into itself thee:same° .1 cycle deed of the previous life. The power or fee whieli is generated by the deods of one earth life siirves to draw the spirit back again into thnearth spilicre,there to under- go the precise counterpart of such •le-d tt Whatsoever a inan soweth, that shall he also rev." The eternal law of Cause and effect holds as good in the spiritual as in the material world. Na evil without its punish- ment, and no gigs' without its reward. This tembing of Reincarnation is the only one that even attempts the solution of the awful problems of human life which we see around us. The spirit can only Ix- nully freed from the bondage of matter after many lives if earnest and increasing endeavours—of constant striving towards an ideal altruism. . . .

Such are some of the more important teachings of Theroophy. They are put forward as theories derived from the teachings of sages and mystics of every religion and every ago. It must, however, be remembered that no creed is required from the 'Theosophist , hot every member is urged so to shape his conduct as personally to promote to the best of his ability the first and princi- pal object of the Society to form the nucleus of an universal brotherhood of humanity." To all who are willing to help no we earnestly appoil. We ask for MO abandonment of faith but of Self. May I add that it will give me very great pleasure to send further particulars to any of your readers who will write to me—Yours obediently,

DIVES AND LAZARUS.

Sit—The correspondence columns in your last i:aue were pregnant with material for reflection on Dm old and j eyer-present subject of Poverty and Riches. The great disparity in the distribution of material blessings in this world, has been a fruitful theme with moralists, from the present time back into the " dint remote." Thi. can. trait haa, of late,been accentuated by the MiS.rif•A of Om great strike in London. Your correspondent Cymro " j draws a parallel loJtween the pittance of some of the I dock labourers, and the inflated emoluments of some of! our aristocratic sinecurists ; but leaves us to draw our ' own conelasions. And my friend and rfoorlant literary j opponent, Mr. John tiandy, grows eloquent in praise jof Count Tolstoi, whose recent work, What to do" he I has been pleased to see you make extracts from. I don't kimw whether Mr. Gandy has read Tolstoi's older work, What I believe." The perusal of that work gave me the Unpression that the author was an impractical entli.iast, or whit comes to the same thing, a religious fanatic, or what some people would prefer to call a thorough going and zealous Christian. Ile advocates the carrying out of the doctrines of Christ literally and entirely. Thus the saying, "Resist not evil," Is to stand as a precept binding upon Christians to suffer even robbery and maltreatment without taking ineauseither for its prevention nr the punishinont of the perpetrators. Now one of three things. Either Tolstoi is a mistaken zealot and haa misunderstood the teat ; or he was 'erect in his rendering of the passage —in which rase there is an entire and insurmountable antagonism between the doctrines of Christianity and what is regarded as the solid foundation of civilized society. Poe if wean' run to resist evil, for what do we mainfain a poßee beret That Tolstoi was ri*lit in his interpretation of the meaning of this particular pa.ssage, I am the mon. inclined to think when I recall other pa.ages and texts wind) gs to show Christianity to lw out of touch with the rational basis of modern society. Take the parable ; of Dive, and Lazarus. Hem we have the rich man sent to hell and the poor man to heaven. And why? Because the one was rich and the other one poor, In the absence of any other reason. we must accept this I very 11.-Jr tiaras being, in the opinion of the founder oil Christianity, an adequate one for the condemnation of one man to eternal torment, and the elevation of the other to the regions of eternal bliss. Hence it would I appear that to posneas a substantial balance at your I bankers is a deadly sin ! And conversely to be idle and ! improvident—the two great factors in beggary—re add appear to be the high road to heaven. We ore told ! notlang as to how Dives acquinsl his wealth, nor 110 W he used it beyond the fact that he fared sumptuously every day, and was clothed in the traditional purple and fine lintaa Now, if this tea deadly sin, alas for Belgravia! This pre:loos doctrine has been before the world now some 1800 years, and still men are as earairetly- engaged as ever in trying to get rid JJf that means of grace poverty —by acquiring soul - destroying filthy lame," which goes to prove that they at least have no very lively faith in the vitality and validity of this doctrine. The fact is, Tastni is a gttcsi example of what Christianity would bring net,, if every Christian J was determined, like hint, to carry out its precepts liter- ' ally. and entirely. We should tend to revert to the impracticable, fanatic, asceticism of the dark eget and modern society would lose what they rightly take to be one of their peculiar blessings—the fruits of tho use of right masoning—steam, electricity, be So I think Count Tolstoi a very poee guide to depend upon in this matter. However well his system may work amongst the peasants of Russia, in a civilised country like this it would be quite out of keeping. Here we allow a man to be as rich as he can get, to wear what he likre, to fare as he likes every day, and indulge in liveritol ser- vantsand splendid njuipmres. and this witlmut consign- ing him to; Hades. The anouraly comes in when this modern Dives mils to church in his e.tly conveyanee , and there calls hisnaelf. as per rubric—. a miserable I sinner." I believe there its kind of Avernus for such men, And its presiding demon is Gout, and thirmgate so J their Purgatory. With your corrrepnedents, I deplore the mirerie s of I Ike Dock Labourers strike, and sincerely hope they may I succeed in getting better wagre for their work. But whilst I am so far in sympathy with them. I must I deprecate the preudresentimental mode of regarding 1i,,, and all such questions. I ask myself what is the main cause of these troubles ? And the answer manes plain and unheaimtingly—over production ; the harvest is plentiful but the labours are superabundant it, rein the sins of the fathers haw:been visited on the Children. Probably the ancestors of these men may have mobbed Malthus. Had they but profited by putting into practice , kin teaching. everybody would now have been the bet- ter for it. I believe it to bra sound maxim that no man has the right to bring more children into the world than lie can maintain in dreencyand comfort. But with such men Any doctrine demanding :wltalenial, and self- I ' restraint is otoredinglyunpopular, and I lookforward to ! the time when society jolts own defence will step in and I j say to mieh—" Out of your rernings a portion shall be ! !set aside in proportion to the number of ynnr and as a provision against the evildays Income." In tliis I way the improvident might be made to provide for them- selves, antis prospective burden taketioff the shoulders of a more worthy, frugal, and saving part at the coin- ! munity.-1 am sir, yours be., DUNN PEERS. Penketh, 11th Sept, 1889.

div.head: PROPOSED BIRMINOHAM_ AND LIVERPOOL 8111 P
div.p: PROPOSED BIRMINOHAM_ AND LIVERPOOL 8111 P

A scheme for constructing a ship canal between liir- : mingham and the Mersey is being actively pushed tor, ward, the survey haying been pot completed and the ; estimates prepared. An entirely new canal will be eon- I structed from itirntinglom, penneating the principal iron and coal centre., of Staffordshire and the Potteries, and uniting with he Weaver Navigation at Winatord, finally communiutting with the Manchester Ship Canal and Die Mersey. The change of levels will be overeotne ' by hydraulic lifts, 'Unita to those in UM. on the Seine and in Ilelgi ll nt It has been decided to increasethe proo posed width of the canal from 60ft. to 721 t., rendering it equal to navigation by vowels of 500 tons burden, an compared with 300 tons as originally proposed. As now estimated. the capital outlay will be nearly £3,000,000 sterling. £250,000 being required for the lilts. Instead of a traffic of 2,000,000 tons per annum, how- ever, the promoters believe it will approach 10,000,000 The Committee are obt g the assont if the land- , Imilers, and, aceonling.to a eorrenpondent, are also sup. ported by the Weaver Navigation Company, the Mall- I chester Ship Callal Company, and the Ifierwy Dick I : [taint. A bill empowering the constniction of the canal- will shortly be promoted in Parliament. A FORTNIGHTS MIS.aION AT LATCHFORD. [BY A CORRF.SPONDEN P.] Ou Sunday, Mr. John Greenwood of the Evanttellxv I lion Socil•tv, London. commenced a fortnight's Mission 'inn the Half at Morrishrook Everything was done to make the visit a sucee,s. The morning's service was fairly well attended, and at night the congregation was I exceedingly good, not less than 250. On each occasion, , Mr. Greenwood spoke with great power. and the hearers I were particularly attentive. At the close of the service, name twin or throe of the workmen engaged in prayer. And one could not help wishing that more of the men , were sober and godly an Gene were--yet thane who know the navvy and who are acquainted with his life, and habits are prepared to make every reasonable allow- ance. The navvy is not all bail ; there are traits in his character highly commendable, and which those with ' higher pmtentions would do well to imitate. For inatanee, it is an unwritten law amongat them that no "butty "shall paasthem when on tramp unaided, if there is a shot in the locker. And if the pocket is empty, they will try and borrow, no that they may help the poor ;fellow Mil° is on the road. Failing thin, they are taken ' to the pogr where a good "tuck in '' is prepared by the landlady, and a night's lodging given, in dot a fresh start may he made on the morrow. In fact, the writer who has spent sane time amougnt the poor fellows in persuaded that it is to a great extent the goodn,ss and liberality of their nature that unrries them into thaw .C.,..ara when their worst aide is seen and when link. went in tastily pronotincol against them When sober, they eat and do behave well, as your readers will now know. It is not saving, too much wham speaking of many of the old lite-lling narvim—men who have la-en born and bred on the work—to say they are gentlemen ,in fustian. For. beneath the rough, uncouth exterior. I there is baiting a lannan, nompathatic heart, and living I in that heart is a desire to aa to others as they would that others should do to them. It is to be hoped the fortnight's services upon which Mr. Greenwood ma., entered will result in great goal, and that very many, I ere the mission shall close, will dedicate themselves I to lied._

When they tried to return they found their retreat by the doorway cut off, and that their only hope of escape was through a window the framework if which was of iron. Hy dint of great exertims, both from within and without the building, a portion of the ironwork woo wrenched away, and Ashhe was dragged through. alniost In dead than olive, and very badly burnt.
